market_context: United States/general English; cooked ground meat comparison with clearly identified lean percentages
title: Ground beef vs. ground turkey: nutrition differences

seo.title: Ground beef vs. turkey: protein, fat, and calories
seo.meta_description: Ground turkey is not always leaner than ground beef. Lean percentage matters as much as species. Compare protein, fat, iron, zinc and calories.
seo.search_intent: Compare ground beef and ground turkey while understanding how lean percentage changes the result.

excerpt: The label matters more than the animal name. Cooked 90/10 ground beef is about 230 calories, 28.5 g protein and 12 g fat per 100 g; cooked 93/7 turkey is about 213 calories, 27.1 g protein and 11.6 g fat. Beef supplies more iron and zinc in these references.
content_html:
Calling ground turkey “leaner” than ground beef can be true or false depending on the package. With ground meat, lean-to-fat percentage often matters as much as the species. Extra-lean beef can contain less fat than a turkey product that includes more fat or skin.

A cooked comparison with the percentages identified

Per 100 g cooked90% lean / 10% fat beef93% lean / 7% fat turkey
Calories~230~213
Protein~28.5 g~27.1 g
Total fat~12.0 g~11.6 g
Iron~3.1 mg~1.6 mg
Zinc~6.8 mg~3.8 mg

These are not identical fat percentages—90/10 versus 93/7—so the comparison represents two common products rather than proving that every difference comes from species alone.

Protein is very similar

The cooked references differ by only about 1.4 g protein per 100 g: 28.5 g for beef and 27.1 g for turkey. At a 150 g cooked serving, that is about 42.7 g versus 40.7 g, a small gap in a full meal.

Fat depends heavily on what you buy

A 93/7 label means the raw product is approximately 93% lean and 7% fat by weight. An 85/15 product declares more than twice the fat percentage of a 93/7 product. That shift can change calories more than switching species while keeping lean percentages similar.

Cooking also removes water and allows some fat to drain away. For that reason, a raw package percentage should not be compared directly with a cooked food-composition value.

Beef stands out for iron and zinc

In the references above, beef provides about 3.1 mg iron and 6.8 mg zinc per 100 g, compared with about 1.6 mg iron and 3.8 mg zinc in turkey. That is nearly twice the iron and roughly 80% more zinc in these specific cooked examples.

What about saturated fat?

Lean turkey often has an advantage when it is compared with higher-fat beef, but the label still matters. The cooked 90/10 beef reference contains roughly 4.7 g saturated fat per 100 g. Turkey values vary with fat percentage and whether skin is included.

What to check on the package

  • Lean/fat percentage: 95/5, 93/7, 90/10, 85/15 and so on.
  • Saturated fat per serving or per 100 g.
  • Sodium if the product is seasoned.
  • Ingredients: plain ground meat is not the same as a formulated burger or patty.

Bottom line

Do not choose beef or turkey on the assumption that one is always leaner. Compare the fat percentage first. With similar lean percentages, calories and protein usually move closer together, while beef generally provides more iron and zinc.

faq.question: Is ground turkey always lower in fat than ground beef?
faq.answer: No. It depends on the lean percentage. A 95/5 beef product can be leaner than an 85/15 turkey product.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: At similar fat levels, both are protein-dense. In the cooked references used here, beef provides about 28.5 g and turkey 27.1 g per 100 g.

faq.question: Which has more iron?
faq.answer: Beef generally does. In these cooked references, beef has about 3.1 mg per 100 g versus about 1.6 mg in turkey.
